objective: Managing stakeholders effectively: identifying and assessing stakeholders, and recognizing cultural factors that affect communication
secondaryObjectives: Preventing communication issues: building stakeholder buy-in at project outset and crafting audience-tailored messaging

The organization, the project, the figures and the people are fictional. The minutes or days each step takes and the effects of each decision are teaching simplifications for exam practice, not measured values.

brief.situation: You manage a hospital extension for a fictional health authority. The site team includes subcontractors from three countries; the hospital stays open next door.
handover: Neighbors complained about noise last month.
Clinical staff were not consulted on the construction phasing.
howItWorks: The board shows the risk register against the appetite, each stakeholder's support in words and the docket.
Move on a week at a time. A decision comes to you at each review; before the first, you can read the evidence.
At the end you write the record and a short reflection.

then.log: Week 2: dust reaches an oncology ward; infection control stops the work for two weeks.
Week 3: the crew misses the milestone it never believed in; the follow-on trades stand idle.
Week 4: night deliveries begin unannounced; the council receives 40 complaints and restricts working hours.

idPrompt.title: Who matters most?
idPrompt.context: The infection control lead wasn't on the list.

choices.label: Add the infection control lead and clinical directors as key stakeholders, assess their needs (dust control near wards), and engage them on phasing
choices.feedback: Identifying and assessing stakeholders finds the ones who can stop the work.

choices.label: Keep the contract parties only
choices.feedback: The people who can stop the work are missing.

choices.label: Engage them if problems arise
choices.feedback: By then the problem has happened.

cultPrompt.title: A 'yes' that means 'no'
cultPrompt.context: A crew agreed to an impossible schedule rather than refuse.

choices.label: Change how commitments are asked: one-to-one planning with the crew lead, asking what the crew needs rather than whether they agree, and written confirmations
choices.feedback: Cultural factors shape how people communicate; adapt so real constraints surface.

choices.label: Add an interpreter at meetings
choices.feedback: Language helps; the cultural reluctance to refuse remains.

choices.label: Hold them to their 'yes'
choices.feedback: The schedule fails and blame follows.

choices.label: Tell neighbors in advance with dates, times and a contact, brief clinical staff on ward impacts, and update patients through the hospital

effects.log: Each audience gets its own message.

choices.feedback: Tailored messages before the work build buy-in and prevent complaints.

parts.label: Stakeholders and culture

parts.label: Messages
parts.criteria: Neighbors, staff and patients informed in advance.
parts.modelAnswer: Neighbors get dates and a contact before night deliveries; clinical staff and patients are briefed through the hospital.

scoring.modelReasoning: Managing stakeholders starts with identifying and assessing them by interest and influence, including those who can stop the work. Cultural factors shape communication, so ask for constraints in ways that let them surface. Audience-tailored messages before the work builds buy-in and prevents issues.
